newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco cos. may pay more after ruling - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco cos. may pay more after ruling - analysts.

text.p: The tobacco industry may face higher costs to settle its war with anti-smoking forces after a U.S. judge ruled that the Food and Drug Administration has some authority to regulate cigarettes.
The ruling may also lead to higher cigarette prices.
"It's probably going to cost them a little more as a result of the ruling," said Allan Kaplan, an analyst at Merrill Lynch. "It certainly swings toward the negative."
He added, "It's obviously raised the stakes for the tobacco companies."
U.S. District Judge William Osteen ruled Friday in Greensboro, N.C., that the FDA can regulate the sale and labeling of cigarettes -- but not promotion and advertising of tobacco products.
Analysts said that perhaps the most damaging aspect of the ruling was Osteen's assertion that nicotine is a drug and that a cigarette is a drug delivery device falling under FDA purview.
"That language will make the settlement talks more difficult," said Diane Temple, an analyst at Salomon Brothers.
Facing the possibility of increased government regulation over its product, the tobacco industry may be willing to pay more money to reach a settlement of its legal troubles, analysts said.

Richard Daynard, a tobacco litigation expert at Northeastern University in Boston, said, "I think courts have mentioned nicotine as a drug in passing, but this is the first time that a court has ruled that nicotine is a drug."
He estimated the ruling could raise the price of cigarettes by $2 a pack.

"In order to raise money for the compensation fund and to reduce smoking among kids, they (tobacco companies) are probably going to have to raise the price of cigarettes $2 a pack, producing $30 to $50 billion a year," he said.

John Coffee, a professor at Columbia Law School, said of the ruling, "I think it probably marginally raises somewhat the likely settlement price the industry will have to pay to achieve a global resolution from, ultimately, Congress."

Tobacco stocks fell after the ruling. Philip Morris Cos. Inc. lost $2.625 to $39 a share, RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., owner of R.J. Reynolds, dropped $2.50 to $29.125, and Loews Corp., which owns the Lorillard tobacco unit, dropped $1.875 to $89.75, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
Many analysts described Osteen's ruling as "mixed" because neither side got everything it wanted.
"It's a mixed bag decision from the standpoint of the tobacco companies," said Emanuel Goldman at PaineWebber. "The FDA is also unhappy. No one is totally happy, or unhappy."
He said he did not believe the ruling would "allow anyone to harden their position...because it wasn't clear cut."
Temple believes the tobacco settlement talks might still "have some adverse surprises" for the industry.
Those negatives could drive down the price of tobacco stocks, "and you would get a chance to buy the stocks more cheaply," she said.
Legal experts said Osteen's ruling must be an especially bitter pill for the tobacco industry because it came from a conservative Republican judge in a court in the heart of tobacco country.
"The industry had the advantage of being able to bring this case in the most favorable forum that they could find," Coffee said.

"The odds would be, if anything, that the next round would be also in the government's favor, and also there may be a somewhat greater prospect that the government's authority over advertising would also be upheld," he said.
The tobacco companies have been negotating with anti-tobacco forces on a possible resolution of hundreds of lawsuits and stricter regulations facing the beleaguered but highly profitable industry.
